# How to Turn a Recurring Chore Into a Reusable AI Prompt Template

> **In short:** You can save a prompt with fixed instructions and blank spaces, then fill in only the details that change each week. Keep the template in a notes file you can copy from. Any AI chat assistant works, though very long templates may need a paid plan on some tools.

By the end of this guide, you'll have a reusable prompt for a task you repeat, such as a weekly status update, a meal plan or a monthly summary. It's for anyone who already knows how to start a chat and send a message, and who keeps writing nearly the same request again and again.

## Before you start

- An AI chat assistant account you already use, plus a notes app or a plain text document where you can save text.
- A recurring task you do at least once a month. Pick one you already know well.
- About 30 minutes the first time, and about two minutes for each reuse afterward.
- Some assistants limit how much text you can send in one chat, so keep your template short enough to paste comfortably.

## Step 1 — Pick the chore and gather three past examples

Choose one repeated task and find the last three times you did it. Open your notes, email drafts or folders and copy the finished versions into one document. Your goal is to see what stays the same across them. Look at the greeting, the order of the sections, the length, and the tone.

Why three? One example can mislead you, because it might include a one-time detail. Three examples reveal the pattern. Once they're side by side, you'll notice what you rewrite every time and what you actually repeat.

**What you'll see:** a single document holding three pieces of text that look similar in shape.

**If it looks different:** if you don't have past versions, write down the steps you usually take and a sample of the result you want. Treat that as your first example.

💬 Example: a sentence to note at the top of your document: "Weekly update for [team name]: wins, blockers, next week."

**You'll know it worked when** you can point to two or three parts of the task that appear in every version.

## Step 2 — Split fixed instructions from changing details

Now mark each part of your examples. Anything that never changes is a fixed instruction, such as "keep it under 150 words" or "start with the three biggest wins." Anything that changes each time is a variable, such as the project name, this week's dates or a list of new numbers.

Use two colors or two symbols, like bold for fixed text and underlining for variables, or simply write the variables in capital letters for now. Don't worry about perfection. You're sorting, not writing the final prompt yet.

**What happens next:** you'll see a clear picture of your template. The fixed part becomes the instructions that never change, and the variable part becomes the blanks you fill each time.

**If it looks different:** if everything seems to change, your task may be too broad. Narrow it to one repeated piece, like only the summary paragraph, and build the template for that.

💬 Example: a fixed instruction you might keep: "Write in a friendly, plain tone. Use no more than five bullet points."

**You'll know it worked when** you have a short list of fixed rules and a short list of blanks.

## Step 3 — Build the template with square-bracket placeholders

Write your prompt in one block. Put the fixed instructions first, then the blanks in square brackets, like [team name] or [paste this week's notes here]. Square brackets are a convention many people use, and they make blanks easy to spot. Keep each bracket to a few words so you can see at a glance what goes there.

Aim for no more than five blanks. More than that and the template becomes hard to fill in, which defeats the time-saving goal.

**What happens next:** you have a single reusable block of text you can copy anywhere.

**If it looks different:** if your template looks messy, check that each bracket has a clear label and that the fixed instructions sit above the blanks.

💬 Example: "Write my weekly status update for [team name]. Start with the three biggest wins from [date range]. Then list blockers, using plain language a non-expert can follow. Keep it under 150 words and end with one question for my manager."

**You'll know it worked when** someone else could read the template and understand what to type into each bracket.

## Step 4 — Run it once and check the result

Open a new chat with your assistant. Paste the template and replace each bracket with real details from this week. Send it. Read the answer as if it were your own work. Ask yourself: is it accurate, does it match my facts, and would I send it without changes?

The assistant only knows what you give it. If you leave a detail out, it may guess, so check every name, date and number against your notes. The assistant can organize and rephrase your information, but it can't confirm that your facts are true.

**What happens next:** the answer appears below your message, usually in a few seconds. Compare it with your three past examples.

**If it looks different:** if the answer is much longer or shorter than you expected, your fixed instructions may be too loose. Adjust them in the next step.

💬 Example: "Here are my notes for this week: [paste your notes here]. Use only these facts, and do not add anything I didn't mention."

**You'll know it worked when** the answer uses your real facts and reads close to the style of your past examples.

## Step 5 — Tighten the rules after each run

Almost every template needs a second pass. Look at what annoyed you in the answer. Maybe it added a sign-off you don't use, or it used a word your team wouldn't say. Add one rule that fixes exactly that problem, such as "Do not include a greeting or sign-off." Then run the template again with the same details.

Change only one thing at a time. If you add five rules at once, you won't know which one helped. Two or three rounds usually produce a template you can trust.

**What happens next:** the new answer should match your intent more closely. If it doesn't, check whether the rule is clear or whether it conflicts with another instruction.

**If it looks different:** if the assistant ignores a rule, move it to the top of the template and repeat it in plain words. Some assistants follow early instructions more reliably.

💬 Example: "Do not include a greeting, a sign-off or any headings. Write the update as plain paragraphs and bullet points only."

**You'll know it worked when** your second run needs fewer manual edits than your first.

## Step 6 — Save the template and reuse it

Save your final template in your notes app or document with a clear name, like "Weekly update template." Some assistants also offer a feature called Projects or custom instructions, where you can keep standing rules for a topic. If your assistant has one, you can paste your fixed instructions there so you only need to type the changing details. Check your assistant's help center for the exact name and how it works, since these features vary and change over time.

Each week, copy the template, fill the blanks and send it. Keep a short note of anything you had to change, and update the template when you notice a pattern.

**What happens next:** the reusable version lets you finish the same task in a few minutes, because the thinking is already done.

**If it looks different:** if your assistant has no Projects or custom instructions feature, the notes-file method still works fine. Copy and paste is all you need.

💬 Example: "Write my weekly status update for [team name]. Use these notes: [paste this week's notes here]. Follow all the rules in my saved instructions."

**You'll know it worked when** you can complete the task in about two minutes, with only a quick check before you send it.

## Common mistakes

- **Overloading the template.** Ten blanks and twelve rules make the prompt slow to fill in and easy to break. The fix is to keep five or fewer blanks and only the rules that really matter.
- **Trusting the output without checking.** The assistant may confidently invent a detail you didn't give it. The fix is to compare every name, number and date against your notes before you send anything.
- **Forgetting to update the template.** Your job changes, and an old template keeps producing old-style results. The fix is to review it once a month and remove rules you no longer need.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** a weekly meal plan template with blanks for [number of people] and [dietary needs] can replace the same planning chat you repeat every Sunday.
- **For your business or work:** a meeting-summary template can turn your rough notes into a clear action list in the same format every time, so teammates know where to look.
- **If you want to go further:** try a two-step template, where the first prompt asks the assistant to list the key facts from your notes, and the second prompt, in the same chat, turns that list into the finished update. Building on earlier answers like this is a useful habit, though the assistant may still need you to check its work.

## Try it now

Open your notes, copy one repeated task into a new document and mark three blanks in square brackets. Then paste the template into your assistant, fill the blanks with one real example and read the answer. Two minutes is enough to see whether the idea saves you time.
